title: Short Stuff: Shark Arm Murders
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Shark Arm murders of 1935 in Sydney, Australia. A tiger shark caught off Cronulla (pronounced variously Coogee/Cronulla in the hosts' discussion) beach vomits up a human arm, which is identified via a tattoo and fingerprints as belonging to Jim Smith, a bankrupt builder turned underworld smuggler, boxer and bookmaker. Investigators link Smith's last known drinking with Patrick Brady to a cab ride to the house of boat builder and smuggler Reginald Holmes. Holmes and Brady are arrested on circumstantial evidence; Holmes attempts suicide in the harbor, leads a four-hour boat chase, then is found dead in his car with three gunshot wounds to the chest. The case against Brady collapses. Theories include Eddie Wayman as the trigger man (Smith allegedly an informant), gangland killings, and Holmes hiring a hitman to fake his death for insurance money. The hosts also discuss the film Fletch and Chevy Chase movies.

segments.title: Intro and setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Shark Arm murders episode and thank their sources, then begin with the story of a fisherman whose tiger shark swallowed a smaller shark off a beach near Sydney.

segments.title: The tiger shark and the arm
segments.summary: The fisherman takes the tiger shark to an aquarium amid recent fatal shark attacks in New South Wales. On Anzac Day, April 25, the shark becomes lethargic and vomits up a human arm. Autopsy shows it was cut with a sharp object, not bitten, and a tattoo and fingerprints lead to Jim Smith.

segments.title: Jim Smith's background
segments.summary: Edwin Smith comes forward believing the arm belonged to his brother, Jim Smith, who had a boxing tattoo. Police confirm the identity and treat it as murder. Jim Smith was a bankrupt builder who worked in the Sydney underworld as a boxer, bookmaker and smuggler.

segments.title: Cab ride and Reginald Holmes
segments.summary: Smith's last known whereabouts were drinking with Patrick Brady at a hotel. A cab driver testifies that Brady took him to the North Sydney house of Reginald Holmes, a boat builder who also smuggled contraband picked up from Sydney Harbour.

segments.title: Motive and circumstantial case
segments.summary: Smith and Holmes reportedly fell out over a smuggling scam, and Smith allegedly blackmailed Holmes. Police theorized Brady killed Smith and brought the arm to Holmes. The arm was thrown back in the ocean and the body presumably sunk. The evidence was circumstantial, so police needed confessions.

segments.title: Holmes's suicide attempt and death
segments.summary: Brady and Holmes are arrested but make no confession. On May 20, Holmes tries to shoot himself in a speedboat, is rescued from the water, and leads police on a four-hour boat chase before surrendering. He then offers to testify against Brady, is allowed to drive off, and is found dead in his car with three gunshot wounds to the chest.

segments.title: Trial collapse and alternate theories
segments.summary: With Holmes dead, the case against Brady collapses; a quick trial ends with the judge unable to proceed on circumstantial evidence. Smith may have been a police informant who informed on Eddie Wayman, a dangerous underworld figure who may have been the trigger man, per author Alex Castle. Other theories include gangland killings of informants and Holmes hiring a hitman to fake his death for insurance money, as Atlas Obscura suggested.

segments.title: Fletch and Chevy Chase tangent
segments.summary: The hosts compare the Holmes hitman theory to the plot of Fletch, in which Tim Matheson's character hires Fletch to kill him. They briefly discuss Chevy Chase films and Neil Simon's Murdered by Death.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and the show credits iHeartRadio.
